subsection: 1. The Vienna settlement and the system of Metternich under attack, 1815–1848

notes.b: The victorious powers after Napoleon met at Vienna to redraw the map of Europe. Their aim was to restore stability and prevent another French bid for dominance.
points: The Congress met from late 1814 and its final Act was signed in June 1815, days before the battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815).
Its leading figures were Metternich for Austria, Castlereagh for Britain, Tsar Alexander I for Russia, Hardenberg for Prussia and Talleyrand for restored France.
The principle of legitimacy meant that rulers deposed by Napoleon were restored, with the Bourbons returned to the French throne.
The balance of power was used to create a ring of states around France: the Kingdom of the Netherlands, enlarged to include Belgium, and Piedmont-Sardinia strengthened in the north-west.
Austria regained control of Lombardy and Venetia in northern Italy and became the dominant power in the peninsula, with Austrian rulers or relatives in several Italian states.
Prussia gained territory in the Rhineland and Westphalia, which made it a guardian of the Rhine frontier against France.
Russia gained most of the Duchy of Warsaw as the Congress Kingdom of Poland, with the Tsar as its king.
Britain kept colonies taken during the wars, including Malta, Heligoland and the Cape Colony, and Castlereagh pressed for a moderate settlement that avoided humiliating France.
The Papal States were restored to the Pope, who regained the central Italian lands he had lost to Napoleon.
The Congress did not give the peoples of Europe a say; it reordered territory largely according to the interests of the great powers.

notes.h: The German Confederation and its Diet
points: The Congress replaced the old Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, with a German Confederation of 39 sovereign states.
The Confederation had a Diet (Bundestag) that met at Frankfurt, where Austria held the presidency.
Its constitution was weak: decisions needed majorities that were difficult to reach, and the member states kept their own armies and rulers.
Austria and Prussia were the two dominant members, and their rivalry shaped German politics for the next half century.
Article 13 of the Federal Act promised member states constitutions, but most rulers never delivered them, which caused liberal anger.
The Diet was made up of delegates sent by the governments of the member states, so the Confederation had no elected national parliament.

notes.h: The Concert of Europe and the Congress System
notes.b: After 1815 the great powers met regularly to manage crises. Metternich used these meetings to suppress revolutions.
points: The Quadruple Alliance of Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia (1815) bound the four to keep France under control and to meet at intervals.
The Holy Alliance of Russia, Austria and Prussia (1815) pledged rulers to govern according to Christian principles; Britain stayed out and the Pope and the Ottoman Sultan were not members.
Congress at Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) ended the Allied army of occupation in France and admitted France to the Concert of Europe, a sign that the powers now trusted restored France.
Congress at Troppau (1820) issued the Troppau Protocol, which allowed intervention against revolutions in states that threatened the European order.
Congress at Laibach (1821) authorised Austrian troops to suppress the revolution in Naples and Piedmont.
Congress at Verona (1822) failed to agree on intervention in Spain, and Britain, under Castlereagh and then Canning, withdrew from the Congress System.
The British withdrawal meant that the Congress System lost its unity from the early 1820s onwards.

notes.b: Metternich, Austria's chancellor from 1821 and its effective ruler, aimed to preserve the 1815 settlement and the Habsburg Empire's multinational structure.
points: Metternich's Austria was an autocracy: there was no constitution, and power rested with the emperor, the Hofkanzlei and a network of police and censors.
The Carlsbad Decrees (August 1819) followed the murder of the dramatist August von Kotzebue by a radical student and were passed by the Diet of the Confederation.
The Carlsbad Decrees imposed censorship of the press, dismissed liberal professors and placed the universities under state supervision.
A central investigation commission was set up at Mainz in 1819 to search out subversive activity in the German states.
The Burschenschaften, student fraternities founded at Jena in 1815, were the main nationalist and liberal student movement that the decrees targeted.
The Six Articles of June 1832, passed after the Hambach Festival, tightened the controls: the Confederation could intervene against disorder and restrict the press and associations.
Metternich used the secret police and informers to watch dissidents, and a strict censorship limited what newspapers and books could print.
His system depended on the cooperation of Prussia and Russia, so the Austrian grip weakened when the two states disagreed.
Metternich, born in 1773, had been Austrian foreign minister from 1809 and became state chancellor in 1821, dominating Habsburg policy until 1848.
His foreign policy rested on keeping Russia and Prussia aligned with Austria against liberal and nationalist movements.
The Wartburg Festival (October 1817) of students celebrated the anniversary of Luther's Reformation and the battle of Leipzig, and called for a united German state.
The Revolutions of 1820–21 in Spain, Naples and Piedmont demanded constitutions and were suppressed with Austrian and other intervention, Spain by French troops in 1823.
The Greek War of Independence began in 1821 against Ottoman rule; European philhellenism led to Russian, British and French intervention and the battle of Navarino (1827).
The July Revolution in France (1830) overthrew Charles X, the last Bourbon king who had tried to rule by decree, and brought Louis-Philippe to power.
The Belgian revolt of August 1830 separated Belgium from the Netherlands; the Great Powers recognised Belgian independence in 1831.
The November Uprising (1830–31) in Russian-controlled Poland was crushed by Russian forces in 1831.
Revolts in central Italy in 1831 against the papal states and the Duchy of Modena were put down with Austrian troops.
The London Protocol of February 1830 recognised an independent Greek state, which was made a monarchy under Otto of Bavaria.
The poet Lord Byron, a supporter of the Greek cause, died at Missolonghi in April 1824, which increased philhellene sympathy in Britain.
The Hambach Festival of May 1832 brought liberals and nationalists together to call for German unity, press freedom and constitutions, and it prompted the Six Articles.
The Prussian Customs Union (Zollverein) was formed in 1834, abolishing internal tariffs among its members and creating a single market.
The Zollverein was the first major German economic union, and its membership grew steadily; Austria was excluded.
Prussia's leadership of the Zollverein gave it an economic basis for leadership of Germany, a challenge to Austria's position.
The Zollverein helped to build railways, roads and trade, and promoted a sense of German economic identity.
Its treaties were agreed in 1833 and took effect on 1 January 1834.
The February Revolution in Paris in 1848 ended the July Monarchy and inspired revolts in German and Austrian cities.
In Vienna, students and citizens demonstrated on 13 March 1848, and Metternich resigned and fled to Britain within days.
Metternich's fall showed that the repressive system depended on the army and police remaining loyal, which was not guaranteed in 1848.
After March 1848 the Austrian government promised a constitution and the Habsburg lands were thrown into a crisis of nationalities, with Hungarian, Czech and Italian demands.
Metternich's departure removed the figure who had led the Congress System and the defence of the 1815 settlement.
Liberals in Germany took up the March events as the start of their own movement, and the Frankfurt Parliament met within two months.

notes.b: Metternich was admired by conservatives and loathed by liberals and nationalists. Historians still disagree about how far he preserved peace or merely delayed change.
points: Conservatives praised his success in keeping Europe free of a general war for almost forty years after 1815.
Liberals and nationalists saw him as the enemy of constitutions, press freedom and national unity, and his censorship made him a symbol of reaction.
Metternich himself argued that the system preserved order and the rights of rulers against revolutionary violence, and his memoirs, published after his death in 1859, defended his policies.
Historians who admire him stress the avoidance of a general European war and the stability of the Habsburg Empire until 1848.
Critics argue that repression did not remove the causes of unrest and that the nationalist movements returned with greater force in 1848 and after.

Assessment: Metternich's system kept the great powers at peace and suppressed most revolutions before 1848, but it failed to meet demands for national unity and constitutions, and it collapsed within days of the Vienna rising.

keyTerms.definition: The principle at the Congress of Vienna that rightful dynasties deposed by Napoleon should be restored to their thrones.
The arrangement of territories and alliances so that no single state could dominate Europe, which the Congress used to contain France.
The post-1815 practice of the great powers meeting at congresses to manage crises and to suppress revolutions that threatened the settlement.
A system of government in which a single ruler holds unlimited power, with no constitution or elected body limiting it.
The 1815–1848 political doctrine that favoured constitutional government, civil liberties and limits on the power of rulers.
The belief that people sharing a language, culture or history should form their own state, which challenged the multinational empires of 1815.
The loose association of 39 German states created in 1815, with a Diet at Frankfurt and Austria as president.
The repressive measures of 1819 that imposed press censorship and state control of universities after the murder of Kotzebue.
A student fraternity founded in 1815 that promoted liberal and nationalist ideas and was targeted by Metternich's repression.
The Prussian-led customs union formed in 1834, which removed internal tariffs among its German members and excluded Austria.
